nodes.title: Structural inequality - Wikipedia
nodes.exact_phrasing: Structural inequality occurs when the fabric of organizations, institutions, governments or social networks contains an embedded cultural, linguistic, economic, religious/belief, physical or identity based bias which provides advantages for some members and marginalizes or produces disadvantages for other members.

nodes.title: Structural Inequality | Definition, Examples & Analysis
nodes.author: Georgie Williams
nodes.exact_phrasing: Structural inequality is defined as a condition that arises out of attributing an unequal status to a category of people in relation to one or more categories of people, a relationship that is perpetuated and reinforced by a confluence of unequal relations in roles, functions, decision rights, and opportunities.
nodes.attribution_text: In Inclusive States: Social Policy and Structural Inequalities

parents.evidence: Perlego study guide on structural inequality draws on the same academic concept of embedded institutional bias; cites 'Inclusive States' scholarship consistent with Wikipedia's sourcing tradition
Similar definitional framing to Penn's structural inequality page, likely drawing from same pool of sources

nodes.title: What Is Structural Inequality? - Center for High Impact Philanthropy - University of Pennsylvania
nodes.exact_phrasing: Structural inequality describes disparities in wealth, resources, and other outcomes that result from discriminatory practices of institutions such as legal, educational, business, government, and health care systems. Structural inequalities result from power imbalances when one group has historically set the rules that intentionally or unintentionally exclude others from access to wealth and resources. Those in positions of economic and political power reap benefits and perpetuate systems that deny those benefits to others.

parents.evidence: Penn's definition of structural inequality closely mirrors Wikipedia's definition of structural inequality, restating the same concept of institutional bias producing differential outcomes

nodes.title: The K-Shaped Economy in 2026
nodes.exact_phrasing: A K-shaped economy describes an economic recovery where different groups or industries experience vastly different outcomes – some thrive and grow, while others struggle or decline. This term was intended to highlight the widening economic inequality during periods of recovery or downturn.
nodes.attribution_text: According to a recent report by the U.S. Bank Economics Research Group, 'The K-economy in 2026: Same story, new amplifiers'

parents.evidence: K-shaped economy framing extends the National Affairs discussion of massive economic shifts producing differential returns to different groups, now formalized into a named economic concept
Builds on the structural labor market change framing from equitablegrowth.org, applied to COVID-era recovery divergence

nodes.author: Anjela Taneja and Harry Bignell
nodes.exact_phrasing: The economy is skewed, as the super-rich profit at the expense of the rest. Their wealth is generally not earned on merit but rather they enjoy the fruits of all our labour. Monopolistic corporations can control markets, set the rules and terms of exchange with other companies and workers. Modern systems and structures continue to transfer wealth from the Global South to North.

framings.label: Neutral
framings.framing_text: The economy contains structural features that benefit some groups more than others.

framings.label: Structural Inequality as Systemic Bias
framings.framing_text: Structural inequality occurs when the fabric of organizations, institutions, governments or social networks contains an embedded cultural, linguistic, economic, religious/belief, physical or identity based bias which provides advantages for some members and marginalizes or produces disadvantages for others.
framings.ideological_tradition: Academic sociology and progressive institutionalism; views inequality as embedded in the design of social and political institutions, perpetuated across time through discriminatory practices and power imbalances.

framings.label: Wealth Extraction and Elite Exploitation
framings.framing_text: The economy is skewed, as the super-rich profit at the expense of the rest. Their wealth is generally not earned on merit but rather they enjoy the fruits of all our labour. Unjust global economic systems and modern structures continue to transfer wealth from the many to the few.
framings.ideological_tradition: Left-progressive and socialist critique; frames economic inequality as the deliberate or systemic upward transfer of wealth from working people to elites, with global racial and gender hierarchies as compounding factors.
characteristic_phrases: baked into the global world order

framings.label: Crony Capitalism Corrupting Free Markets
framings.framing_text: Cronyist policies — from tax loopholes to regulatory advantages to direct subsidies — deliberately tilt the playing field. Policy privilege corrupts the free market by rewarding political connections over competitive excellence. Capitalism featuring undue alliances between business interests and politicians.
framings.ideological_tradition: Free-market conservatism and libertarianism; locates the problem not in markets themselves but in government-business collusion that distorts competition and privileges insiders over ordinary participants.

framings.label: Uneven Transaction Costs and Political Capture
framings.framing_text: The value of resources is maximized for those who face low transaction costs, but not for those who face high transaction costs. This uneven distribution of transaction costs exists in political systems as well — well-organized groups gain systematic advantages over diffuse, less-organized ones.
framings.ideological_tradition: Institutional economics and public choice theory; uses a neutral analytical lens to explain how differential access to markets and political systems, rather than malice, produces structurally unequal outcomes.

framings.label: Divergent Economic Outcomes as Measurable Phenomenon
framings.framing_text: A K-shaped economy describes an economic recovery where different groups or industries experience vastly different outcomes — some thrive and grow, while others struggle or decline. Massive shifts over the last several decades have changed the nature of work and the returns to different skillsets in ways policymakers didn't anticipate.
framings.ideological_tradition: Technocratic centrism and policy analysis; treats unequal outcomes as an observable, measurable economic pattern driven by structural shifts, framing the issue as a policy challenge rather than a moral or political one.
